cardMetadata.excerpt: Regarded by wildlife biologists, photographers, and rural communities as the tallest and most magnificent wild tusker roaming the island in modern decades. Kawanthissa possessed extraordinary physical stature, standing nearly 11 feet tall with heavy, outward-swept ivory tusks. He represented the pinnacle of dry-zone pachyderm genetics in the northwestern province.

specimens.overview: Regarded by wildlife biologists, photographers, and rural communities as the tallest and most magnificent wild tusker roaming the island in modern decades. Kawanthissa possessed extraordinary physical stature, standing nearly 11 feet tall with heavy, outward-swept ivory tusks. He represented the pinnacle of dry-zone pachyderm genetics in the northwestern province.
narrative: Kawanthissa was named after ancient King Kavantissa of Ruhuna (father of King Dutugemunu), honoring his regal bearing and undisputed dominance across the Galgamuwa tank cascade ecosystem.

In late September 2026, Kawanthissa was discovered limping heavily in the Usgala scrub jungle, dragging his right front leg. Wildlife veterinarians from the Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC), led by senior veterinary surgeons, confirmed a severe gunshot wound penetrating the right foreleg knee joint—believed to be inflicted by a heavy-bore poacher's trap firearm.

For over three weeks, multi-agency veterinary teams camped in the field, administering daily antibiotic darting, localized antiseptic washing, and vitamin injections. While swelling initially showed slight reduction, systemic septicemia set in.

On October 15, 2026, weakened from refusing feed and water, Kawanthissa collapsed in a muddy paddy field in the Siyambalangamuwa area. Villagers, wildlife officers, and civil defense personnel rallied with heavy machinery, canvas slings, and water pumps to keep his massive body hydrated and shaded.

Tragically, despite emergency intravenous cardiopulmonary resuscitation, Kawanthissa passed away at 6:18 PM on October 16, 2026. His death ignited widespread national mourning and outrage. A joint raid by the Walana Anti-Corruption Unit and DWC subsequently arrested a suspect with two firearms, and Environment Minister Dr. Dammika Patabendi ordered an independent national inquiry into the incident.

timeline.detail: Photographed extensively by naturalists; celebrated for never displaying aggression toward rural farming villages when unprovoked.

timeline.title: Gunshot Injury Detected
timeline.detail: DWC field rangers find Kawanthissa immobilized near Usgala with heavy ballistic trauma to the right foreleg.

timeline.title: Intensive Veterinary Intervention
timeline.detail: Over 20 darting sessions delivering high-potency antibiotics, anti-inflammatories, and pain-management therapies.

timeline.title: Passing at 6:18 PM & National Inquest
timeline.detail: Breathed his last surrounded by veterinarians; post-mortem autopsy performed; ministerial investigation launched.

specimens.veterinaryNotes: Post-mortem necropsy confirmed a lead ballistic projectile lodged within the carpals of the right forelimb, resulting in chronic suppurative osteomyelitis and fatal secondary septicemic shock. Severe muscle necrosis along the brachial plexus prevented weight-bearing.
specimens.causeOfDeath: Severe suppurative osteomyelitis, compound joint necrosis, and systemic septicemia secondary to illegal trap-gun ballistic injury.
specimens.legacy: Kawanthissa's tragic death has catalyzed a nationwide campaign demanding the immediate gazetting of the National Tusker Protection Taskforce, mandatory penal increases for trap-gun deployment, and dedicated satellite telemetry tracking for Sri Lanka's remaining wild tuskers.

cardMetadata.excerpt: Sri Lanka's most closely monitored living wild tusker. Agbo is a legendary solitary bull elephant of the ancient tank cascades of Anuradhapura who became a national hero in 2023 when he survived life-threatening gunshot injuries through an unprecedented multi-month veterinary rescue operation.

specimens.overview: Sri Lanka's most closely monitored living wild tusker. Agbo is a legendary solitary bull elephant of the ancient tank cascades of Anuradhapura who became a national hero in 2023 when he survived life-threatening gunshot injuries through an unprecedented multi-month veterinary rescue operation.
narrative: Agbo is a solitary icon of the dry-zone forest patches connecting Thirappane to the ancient Kalawewa reservoir. In June 2023, he was discovered with severe bullet wounds in his left foreleg, leaving him completely incapacitated and trapped in a forest waterhole.

A historic intervention headed by DWC veterinary surgeon Dr. Chandana Jayasinghe and field teams spanned over eight months. The team administered over 35 distinct darting treatments, excavating mud sumps to allow him to stand and flush the deep necrotic wound cavity.

In late 2023, following surgical debridement and miraculous tissue healing, a satellite GPS collar was fitted to track his movements, prevent retaliatory human-elephant conflicts, and ensure continuous health audits.
Today, Agbo roams the perimeter of Kalawewa National Park, feeding on riparian grasses and bathing regularly in ancient waterways, monitored continuously by local DWC tracking teams.

specimens.veterinaryNotes: Extensive deep tissue bullet wound in left carpus; required multiple field surgical debridements, long-acting oxytetracycline administration, and topical antiseptic flushes. Patient is ambulatory with mild chronic stiffness.
specimens.legacy: Stands as an inspiring beacon of hope in Asian wildlife medicine, demonstrating that high-level field orthopedic care and multi-month dedicated veterinary commitment can save wild adult bull elephants.

cardMetadata.excerpt: Named after the revered ancient monarch King Mahasen (who engineered the Great Minneriya Tank in 276–303 CE), this imposing wild patriarch is the crowning jewel of the annual Minneriya Elephant Gathering.

specimens.overview: Named after the revered ancient monarch King Mahasen (who engineered the Great Minneriya Tank in 276–303 CE), this imposing wild patriarch is the crowning jewel of the annual Minneriya Elephant Gathering.
narrative: King Mahasen constructed the Minneriya reservoir in the 3rd century CE, transforming the dry zone into a fertile heartland. The wild tusker carrying his name is the reigning genetic titan of this ancient water body.

During the dry season (July to October), the 'Minneriya Elephant Gathering' brings together over 300 wild elephants to feed on the sweet, fresh grasses emerging from the receding tank bed. Mahasen enters full musth during this window.

With temporal glands exuding strong pheromonal musk, Mahasen displays undisputed dominance over non-tusked 'Aliya' bulls twice his body width, serving as the prime breeding sire of the Polonnaruwa regional population.
Despite his fierce territorial supremacy during musth, he exhibits an astonishing tolerance of ethical wildlife safari vehicles adhering to the DWC 20-meter boundary protocol.

cardMetadata.excerpt: A mythic wild tusker celebrated for his extraordinarily rare 'Dala Poottuwa' morphology—tusks that crossed over each other symmetrically in front of his trunk. His brutal slaying by poachers in 2017 became the turning point in Sri Lankan wildlife law enforcement.

specimens.overview: A mythic wild tusker celebrated for his extraordinarily rare 'Dala Poottuwa' morphology—tusks that crossed over each other symmetrically in front of his trunk. His brutal slaying by poachers in 2017 became the turning point in Sri Lankan wildlife law enforcement.
narrative: In Sinhala folklore, an elephant whose tusks cross like two crossed swords is termed 'Dala Poottuwa'—a creature prophesied to bring prosperity to its homeland. The Galgamuwa Dala Poottuwa was the living embodiment of this legendary trait.

In his later years, old shotgun pellet wounds caused bilateral cataracts, rendering him virtually blind. Despite his impairment, he peacefully roamed the farming villages of Galgamuwa, guided solely by scent, hearing, and the deep memory of the ancient tank pathways.
In November 2017, he vanished from his habitual foraging grounds. A massive search operation involving air force drones, intelligence officers, and villagers commenced.

On November 29, 2017, police apprehended poachers possessing carved ivory bead charms (Gaja Muthu) and bloodied tusks. Forensic DNA testing conducted by the Peradeniya University Veterinary Faculty conclusively verified the ivory belonged to the beloved Galgamuwa giant.
The national outcry ignited historic legal reforms, stiffer penalties for wildlife crimes, and the destruction of seized ivory stashes by the government.

cardMetadata.excerpt: Asia's tallest tamed tusker of the 21st century and an undisputed national hero. Declared a National Cultural Treasure by Presidential decree, Nadungamuwa Raja served as the Chief Relic Bearer of the Sacred Tooth Relic casket for 15 consecutive seasons.

specimens.overview: Asia's tallest tamed tusker of the 21st century and an undisputed national hero. Declared a National Cultural Treasure by Presidential decree, Nadungamuwa Raja served as the Chief Relic Bearer of the Sacred Tooth Relic casket for 15 consecutive seasons.
narrative: Nadungamuwa Raja was born in 1953 in the kingdom of Mysore, India. He was gifted by the Maharaja of Mysore to an eminent Ayurvedic physician monk of Nilammahara Temple in Piliyandala, in gratitude for curing a royal relative's chronic illness.
In 1978, he was acquired by renowned Ayurvedic physician Dharmavijaya Veda Ralahamy of Nadungamuwa, Gampaha, where he was nurtured under supreme traditional care.

Standing at a towering 10.5 feet with majestic tusks curving toward the earth, he satisfied all physical markers of the mythical 'Chaddanta' caste: a flat, level spine, an arched neck, a majestic trunk, and unshakeable serenity.

From 2006 to 2021, he carried the sacred Golden Karanduwa (Casket) of the Sacred Tooth Relic at the Kandy Esala Perahera. Remarkably, because he could not travel in motor trucks, he undertook a 90-kilometer pilgrimage on foot from Gampaha to Kandy every year, walking along highways escorted by police commandos and thousands of adoring devotees.

On March 7, 2022, he passed away peacefully at the age of 69. The President of Sri Lanka declared him a National Cultural Treasure and deployed military honors for his funeral. His preserved body is prepared for public display at his ancestral residence in Nadungamuwa.

cardMetadata.excerpt: The most famous sacred elephant in the modern history of Buddhism. Maligawa Raja served as the Chief Relic Bearer of the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic for an astounding 50 years without a single behavioral infraction.

specimens.overview: The most famous sacred elephant in the modern history of Buddhism. Maligawa Raja served as the Chief Relic Bearer of the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic for an astounding 50 years without a single behavioral infraction.
narrative: Captured in 1925 in the deep jungle forests of Batticaloa by veteran elephant trapper Umaru Lebbe Panicker, Raja was purchased by Tikiri Banda Ratwatte Dissawa of Mahaiyawa. In August 1937, he was dedicated as an offering to the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic (Sri Dalada Maligawa).

For an incredible half-century (1937–1987), Raja carried the revered Golden Casket (Karanduwa) containing the Sacred Tooth Relic during the world-renowned Kandy Esala Perahera. His composed poise amidst crackling fire whips, hundreds of dancing torches, exploding firecrackers, and booming drums was legendary.

He exhibited unmatched reverence: if the heavy golden casket tilted even a fraction of an inch, Raja would stand perfectly still in the middle of the procession, refusing to step forward until the Diyawadana Nilame adjusted the relic securely upon his velvet howdah.
On August 20, 1986, President J.R. Jayewardene declared Maligawa Raja a 'National Monument'—the only time an animal in modern history has received such an honor while still living.

When Raja passed away on July 16, 1988 at the age of approximately 75, Sri Lanka declared a national day of mourning. His preserved taxidermied body, adorned with his regal tusks, was enshrined in a special memorial museum within the Maligawa courtyard.

specimens.overview: The reigning supreme temple tusker of Sri Lanka. Indi Raja carries the golden Karanduwa in the Kandy Esala Perahera today, inheriting the mantle of Maligawa Raja and Nadungamuwa Raja.
narrative: In 1987, Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi presented young Indi Raja as a state gift to the people of Sri Lanka, destined to be dedicated to the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic in Kandy.
Reared within the sacred precincts of the temple under the strict guidance of expert traditional mahouts, Indi Raja developed an exceptional aristocratic composure.
Following the demise of the veteran bearers, Indi Raja ascended to the pinnacle role of the Kandy Esala Perahera, carrying the Sacred Casket of the Tooth Relic down the torch-lit streets of Kandy.
His imposing silhouette, symmetrical ivory, and poised gait have earned him widespread reverence across the island and international recognition as the spiritual successor to Maligawa Raja.

cardMetadata.excerpt: Famous throughout the zoological world for possessing the longest tusks recorded on any living Asian elephant in the 20th and 21st centuries, measuring an incredible 7.5 feet each.

specimens.overview: Famous throughout the zoological world for possessing the longest tusks recorded on any living Asian elephant in the 20th and 21st centuries, measuring an incredible 7.5 feet each.
narrative: Captured in 1945 in the dense forests of Nawagaththegama in Anamaduwa, Millangoda Raja was purchased by the aristocratic elephant owner M.R.A. Millangoda of Rambukkana.

Over the decades, his tusks grew to phenomenal lengths, eventually reaching 7 feet 6 inches (2.30 meters). They were so long that when he walked with his head held upright, the ivory tips gracefully grazed the gravel before him.
Millangoda Raja participated in the Kandy Esala Perahera for nearly 40 seasons, carrying the Sacred Casket of Relics on numerous occasions.

When he passed away on July 30, 2011 at the age of 73, zoologists from across the globe commemorated his record-breaking anatomy. His mounted remains and monumental tusks are preserved at the Millangoda ancestral museum in Rambukkana.

cardMetadata.excerpt: The beloved chief sacred tusker dedicated to the shrine of God Skanda-Murugan in the holy city of Kataragama.

specimens.overview: The beloved chief sacred tusker dedicated to the shrine of God Skanda-Murugan in the holy city of Kataragama.
narrative: Dedicated in youth to the ancient shrine of God Kataragama (Skanda-Murugan), Wasana is the sovereign guardian of religious rituals in southern Sri Lanka.

For over two decades, Wasana has carried the sacred deity casket across the revered Menik Ganga during the torchlit Kataragama Esala Festival, a ceremony demanding supreme composure amidst tens of thousands of chanting devotees and fire-walkers.
Renowned for his serene temperament and affectionate rapport with his lifelong mahout, Wasana spends off-season months browsing the riverine foliage bordering the holy city and Yala National Park.
He is revered as a living symbol of spiritual protection and harmonious co-existence between elephants and religious devotion in the deep south.

specimens.overview: A revered temple tusker whose owner took the visionary step of donating his entire skeleton to science, where it stands today as the premier zoological exhibit in the National Museum of Colombo.
narrative: Captured in 1925 in the deep forests of the Eastern Province (near Kattankudy), Heiyantuduwa Raja was acquired by prominent landowner and philanthropist Henry Dharmasena of Heiyantuduwa.

Over four decades, he served as the Chief Relic Bearer of the Kelaniya Duruthu Perahera and was also a distinguished participant in the Kandy Esala Perahera. His 7.5-foot ivory curved in an exquisite crescent shape.
When Raja passed away on November 6, 2002 at the extraordinary age of 78, his owner fulfilled a visionary pledge by donating the entire elephant's remains to the Department of National Museums.

A team of zoologists and taxidermists carefully articulated his complete skeleton. Today, he stands as the centerpiece exhibit in the National Museum of Colombo, offering students, researchers, and visitors an incomparable education in elephant anatomy.

historicalLegends.name: Kandula (Royal War Elephant of King Dutugemunu)
historicalLegends.source: Mahavamsa (The Great Chronicle of Sri Lanka) & Epigraph #LK-AN-04
historicalLegends.significance: The most legendary elephant in ancient Sri Lankan chronicles. Kandula was born on the same day as Prince Dutugemunu and brought by a fisherman to King Kavantissa. In the historic battle of Vijithapura, Kandula heroously battered down the fortress's iron-clad southern gate while braving molten pitch, securing the unification of ancient Sri Lanka.

Tragically, despite emergency intravenous cardiopulmonary resuscitation, Kawanthissa passed away at 6:18 PM on October 16, 2026. His death ignited widespread national mourning and outrage. A joint raid by the Walana Anti-Corruption Unit and DWC subsequently arrested a suspect with two firearms, and Environment Minister Dr. Dammika Patabendi ordered an independent national inquiry into the incident.

agbo-thirappane.overview: Sri Lanka's most closely monitored living wild tusker. Agbo is a legendary solitary bull elephant of the ancient tank cascades of Anuradhapura who became a national hero in 2023 when he survived life-threatening gunshot injuries through an unprecedented multi-month veterinary rescue operation.
narrative: Agbo is a solitary icon of the dry-zone forest patches connecting Thirappane to the ancient Kalawewa reservoir. In June 2023, he was discovered with severe bullet wounds in his left foreleg, leaving him completely incapacitated and trapped in a forest waterhole.

A historic intervention headed by DWC veterinary surgeon Dr. Chandana Jayasinghe and field teams spanned over eight months. The team administered over 35 distinct darting treatments, excavating mud sumps to allow him to stand and flush the deep necrotic wound cavity.

In late 2023, following surgical debridement and miraculous tissue healing, a satellite GPS collar was fitted to track his movements, prevent retaliatory human-elephant conflicts, and ensure continuous health audits.
Today, Agbo roams the perimeter of Kalawewa National Park, feeding on riparian grasses and bathing regularly in ancient waterways, monitored continuously by local DWC tracking teams.

mahasen.overview: Named after the revered ancient monarch King Mahasen (who engineered the Great Minneriya Tank in 276–303 CE), this imposing wild patriarch is the crowning jewel of the annual Minneriya Elephant Gathering.
narrative: King Mahasen constructed the Minneriya reservoir in the 3rd century CE, transforming the dry zone into a fertile heartland. The wild tusker carrying his name is the reigning genetic titan of this ancient water body.

During the dry season (July to October), the 'Minneriya Elephant Gathering' brings together over 300 wild elephants to feed on the sweet, fresh grasses emerging from the receding tank bed. Mahasen enters full musth during this window.

With temporal glands exuding strong pheromonal musk, Mahasen displays undisputed dominance over non-tusked 'Aliya' bulls twice his body width, serving as the prime breeding sire of the Polonnaruwa regional population.
Despite his fierce territorial supremacy during musth, he exhibits an astonishing tolerance of ethical wildlife safari vehicles adhering to the DWC 20-meter boundary protocol.

dala-poottuwa.overview: A mythic wild tusker celebrated for his extraordinarily rare 'Dala Poottuwa' morphology—tusks that crossed over each other symmetrically in front of his trunk. His brutal slaying by poachers in 2017 became the turning point in Sri Lankan wildlife law enforcement.
narrative: In Sinhala folklore, an elephant whose tusks cross like two crossed swords is termed 'Dala Poottuwa'—a creature prophesied to bring prosperity to its homeland. The Galgamuwa Dala Poottuwa was the living embodiment of this legendary trait.

In his later years, old shotgun pellet wounds caused bilateral cataracts, rendering him virtually blind. Despite his impairment, he peacefully roamed the farming villages of Galgamuwa, guided solely by scent, hearing, and the deep memory of the ancient tank pathways.
In November 2017, he vanished from his habitual foraging grounds. A massive search operation involving air force drones, intelligence officers, and villagers commenced.

On November 29, 2017, police apprehended poachers possessing carved ivory bead charms (Gaja Muthu) and bloodied tusks. Forensic DNA testing conducted by the Peradeniya University Veterinary Faculty conclusively verified the ivory belonged to the beloved Galgamuwa giant.
The national outcry ignited historic legal reforms, stiffer penalties for wildlife crimes, and the destruction of seized ivory stashes by the government.

nadungamuwa-raja.overview: Asia's tallest tamed tusker of the 21st century and an undisputed national hero. Declared a National Cultural Treasure by Presidential decree, Nadungamuwa Raja served as the Chief Relic Bearer of the Sacred Tooth Relic casket for 15 consecutive seasons.
narrative: Nadungamuwa Raja was born in 1953 in the kingdom of Mysore, India. He was gifted by the Maharaja of Mysore to an eminent Ayurvedic physician monk of Nilammahara Temple in Piliyandala, in gratitude for curing a royal relative's chronic illness.
In 1978, he was acquired by renowned Ayurvedic physician Dharmavijaya Veda Ralahamy of Nadungamuwa, Gampaha, where he was nurtured under supreme traditional care.

Standing at a towering 10.5 feet with majestic tusks curving toward the earth, he satisfied all physical markers of the mythical 'Chaddanta' caste: a flat, level spine, an arched neck, a majestic trunk, and unshakeable serenity.

From 2006 to 2021, he carried the sacred Golden Karanduwa (Casket) of the Sacred Tooth Relic at the Kandy Esala Perahera. Remarkably, because he could not travel in motor trucks, he undertook a 90-kilometer pilgrimage on foot from Gampaha to Kandy every year, walking along highways escorted by police commandos and thousands of adoring devotees.

On March 7, 2022, he passed away peacefully at the age of 69. The President of Sri Lanka declared him a National Cultural Treasure and deployed military honors for his funeral. His preserved body is prepared for public display at his ancestral residence in Nadungamuwa.

cardMetadata.excerpt: The most famous sacred elephant in the modern history of Buddhism. Maligawa Raja served as the Chief Relic Bearer of the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic for an astounding 50 years without a single behavioral infraction.

maligawa-raja.overview: The most famous sacred elephant in the modern history of Buddhism. Maligawa Raja served as the Chief Relic Bearer of the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic for an astounding 50 years without a single behavioral infraction.
narrative: Captured in 1925 in the deep jungle forests of Batticaloa by veteran elephant trapper Umaru Lebbe Panicker, Raja was purchased by Tikiri Banda Ratwatte Dissawa of Mahaiyawa. In August 1937, he was dedicated as an offering to the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic (Sri Dalada Maligawa).

For an incredible half-century (1937–1987), Raja carried the revered Golden Casket (Karanduwa) containing the Sacred Tooth Relic during the world-renowned Kandy Esala Perahera. His composed poise amidst crackling fire whips, hundreds of dancing torches, exploding firecrackers, and booming drums was legendary.

He exhibited unmatched reverence: if the heavy golden casket tilted even a fraction of an inch, Raja would stand perfectly still in the middle of the procession, refusing to step forward until the Diyawadana Nilame adjusted the relic securely upon his velvet howdah.
On August 20, 1986, President J.R. Jayewardene declared Maligawa Raja a 'National Monument'—the only time an animal in modern history has received such an honor while still living.

When Raja passed away on July 16, 1988 at the age of approximately 75, Sri Lanka declared a national day of mourning. His preserved taxidermied body, adorned with his regal tusks, was enshrined in a special memorial museum within the Maligawa courtyard.

narrative: In 1987, Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi presented young Indi Raja as a state gift to the people of Sri Lanka, destined to be dedicated to the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic in Kandy.
Reared within the sacred precincts of the temple under the strict guidance of expert traditional mahouts, Indi Raja developed an exceptional aristocratic composure.
Following the demise of the veteran bearers, Indi Raja ascended to the pinnacle role of the Kandy Esala Perahera, carrying the Sacred Casket of the Tooth Relic down the torch-lit streets of Kandy.
His imposing silhouette, symmetrical ivory, and poised gait have earned him widespread reverence across the island and international recognition as the spiritual successor to Maligawa Raja.

millangoda-raja.overview: Famous throughout the zoological world for possessing the longest tusks recorded on any living Asian elephant in the 20th and 21st centuries, measuring an incredible 7.5 feet each.
narrative: Captured in 1945 in the dense forests of Nawagaththegama in Anamaduwa, Millangoda Raja was purchased by the aristocratic elephant owner M.R.A. Millangoda of Rambukkana.

Over the decades, his tusks grew to phenomenal lengths, eventually reaching 7 feet 6 inches (2.30 meters). They were so long that when he walked with his head held upright, the ivory tips gracefully grazed the gravel before him.
Millangoda Raja participated in the Kandy Esala Perahera for nearly 40 seasons, carrying the Sacred Casket of Relics on numerous occasions.

When he passed away on July 30, 2011 at the age of 73, zoologists from across the globe commemorated his record-breaking anatomy. His mounted remains and monumental tusks are preserved at the Millangoda ancestral museum in Rambukkana.

narrative: Captured in 1925 in the deep forests of the Eastern Province (near Kattankudy), Heiyantuduwa Raja was acquired by prominent landowner and philanthropist Henry Dharmasena of Heiyantuduwa.

Over four decades, he served as the Chief Relic Bearer of the Kelaniya Duruthu Perahera and was also a distinguished participant in the Kandy Esala Perahera. His 7.5-foot ivory curved in an exquisite crescent shape.
When Raja passed away on November 6, 2002 at the extraordinary age of 78, his owner fulfilled a visionary pledge by donating the entire elephant's remains to the Department of National Museums.

A team of zoologists and taxidermists carefully articulated his complete skeleton. Today, he stands as the centerpiece exhibit in the National Museum of Colombo, offering students, researchers, and visitors an incomparable education in elephant anatomy.
